title: GCD of Two Numbers
directAnswer: Apply Euclid: while `b != 0`, set `(a, b) = (b, a % b)`. When `b` hits 0, `a` is the GCD. O(log(min(a,b))).

remember.takeaway: Euclid replaces a divisor search with a handful of mod steps.
remember.formula: while b != 0: a, b = b, a % b;  return a

problemStatement: Given two non-negative integers `a` and `b` (not both zero), return their greatest common divisor.
understanding: The Euclidean algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), shrinking the pair until one becomes 0.

approaches.name: Euclidean algorithm
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
The Euclidean algorithm computes gcd(a, b) by repeatedly replacing the pair with `(b, a mod b)` until the second number is 0; the remaining first number is the GCD.

**Why `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)`.** Any number that divides both a and b also divides `a − k·b = a mod b`, and vice versa — so the pair (a, b) and the pair (b, a mod b) share *exactly* the same set of common divisors, hence the same greatest one. Each step shrinks the numbers fast, so it terminates quickly.

**Why it ends in O(log) steps.** The remainder at least halves every two steps, so the number of iterations is logarithmic in min(a, b) — vastly faster than testing every candidate divisor.

**The base case.** When b becomes 0, a holds the answer, and `gcd(x, 0) = x` is exactly right (every number divides 0). That's why the loop condition is `while (b != 0)` and the result is the final a.
hints: Common divisors of a and b are the same as common divisors of b and (a mod b).
Repeatedly do (a, b) = (b, a % b) until b is 0.
When b hits 0, a is the GCD — no divisor search needed.
approaches.insight: Euclid is dramatically faster than trying every divisor — mention the log complexity.
approaches.complexityReasoning: the remainder shrinks geometrically, so it terminates in O(log(min(a,b))) steps.

java.explanation: Replace the pair with (b, a mod b), preserving the GCD.

dryRun.intro: Replace the pair with (b, a mod b) each step.

edgeCases.behavior: gcd(0, 5) = 5; the loop returns b's value via one swap.
Equal → gcd 12 after one step (12 mod 12 = 0).

pitfalls: Searching every divisor (O(min(a,b))) instead of using Euclid.
Mishandling the gcd(x, 0) = x base case.

commonMistakes: Looping over all divisors (O(min(a,b))) instead of using Euclid.
Mishandling the gcd(x, 0) = x base case.

followupVariations.title: LCM of Two Numbers
followupVariations.hint: lcm = a / gcd * b, reusing this.

followupVariations.title: GCD of an Array
followupVariations.hint: Fold gcd across all elements; gcd is associative.

patternNote: A core fresher pattern: Euclidean reduction. Master it on small inputs and it transfers to harder problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know Euclid's algorithm and can justify why mod-reduction preserves the GCD.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: A brute-force divisor scan, or breaking the (x, 0) base case.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain the shared-divisor invariant and note that LCM builds on this.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can either input be 0?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — gcd(x, 0) = x; the algorithm handles it naturally if not both are 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need the extended version (coefficients)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only if asked; the extended Euclid also returns x, y with ax + by = gcd.
